The 50% upper limit on under-12m maturities is unusually permissive — most councils cap it far lower — and it accommodates the strategy's stated intent to use short-term borrowing when rates are expected to fall. facts.value: The chart at p.17 shows a long-term under-borrowed position, with existing PWLB stock c.£370m and market loans (excl LOBO) c.£120m and LOBOs c.£30m at 2025, all running off to zero by around 2076-79; §1.49 states 'The Benchmark for North Tyneside Council demonstrates a long-term under borrowed position. This aligns with the current strategy to minimise long-term external borrowing costs by using internal borrowing'

source.title: Prudential Indicators 2026-2031 — Appendix B(iii) to the 2026/27 budget pack, Council, 12 February 2026

facts.value: Strategy is priced against Bank Rate at 4% — §4.1 notes cuts from 4.50% to 4.25% in May 2025 and to 4% in August 2025, and holds at 4% in September and November 2025; §5.1 frames the strategy around rates 'on a downwards trajectory'; §5.2 anticipates 'long-term borrowing rates to remain stagnant over the next few years'

source.title: Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27 — Appendix C, Council, 12 February 2026

facts.value: §5.2 priority order for new borrowing: (1) internal borrowing first — 'the cheapest borrowing and lowest risk approach'; (2) temporary borrowing from money markets or other LAs; (3) long-term fixed rate market loans 'at rates significantly below PWLB rates for the equivalent maturity period (where available)'; (4) PWLB borrowing for periods under 10 years; (5) PWLB borrowing longer than 10 years 'may be explored'

source.title: Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27 — Appendix C, Council, 12 February 2026

facts.note: The order and language is standard MUFG-shop treasury strategy. Notable that item (3) allows for long-term market loans below PWLB — most councils allow this in principle but rarely find market loans below PWLB in practice. Item (4) preferring sub-10y PWLB is explicit.

facts.value: §7.1 acknowledges 'potential opportunities to generate savings by switching from long-term debt to short-term debt' but notes 'these savings will need to be considered in the light of the current treasury position and the size of the cost of debt repayment (premiums incurred)'; §7.2 keeps the strategy flexible; §7.3 requires all rescheduling to be reported to Cabinet at the next available meeting

source.title: Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27 — Appendix C, Council, 12 February 2026

facts.note: The phrase 'premiums incurred' is right for a book where most loans sit below par, but our indicative DMO curve says otherwise — of 62 PWLB loans on their book, 57 are at a discount and only 5 at a premium. summary.text:
Read on the 2026/27 Treasury Management Strategy pack that went to Cabinet on 26 January 2026 and Full Council on 12 February 2026 — three appendices: C (the strategy narrative, 11 pages), B(iii) (Prudential Indicators 2026-2031, 18 pages, which is where all the balance-sheet figures live), and D (Treasury Management Practices, 30 pages of CIPFA boilerplate with nothing quantitative except the £1m Barclays overdraft and the MUFG contract dates).

The balance-sheet identity in Appendix B(iii) Table 3 foots exactly in every one of the six forecast years: CFR less external borrowing less other long-term liabilities closes to the implied internal-borrowing position to the £000. What that arithmetic shows is the hook. External borrowing runs down from £528.4m at 31.03.26 to £431.4m at 31.03.31 — a £97m reduction, largely PWLB naturally maturing. Other long-term liabilities (PFI and finance leases) fall from £140.7m to £87.7m as those schemes run off. But the CFR only drops from £692.7m to £646.7m over the same period, a £46m fall. The gap is the growing under-borrowed position, from £23.6m at 31.03.26 to £127.6m at 31.03.31 — a 5.4x rise.

Appendix C §5.1 is honest about the trade: the CFR 'has not been fully funded with loan debt as cash supporting the Authority's reserves, balances and cash flow has been used as a temporary measure. However, with interest rates on a downwards trajectory, the Authority has to review borrowing requirements whilst considering the risk of interest rates rising.' §5.2 sets internal borrowing as the top-priority funding source and explicitly anticipates 'long-term borrowing rates to remain stagnant over the next few years.' The strategy is priced against Bank Rate at 4% (§4.1 mentions the May and August 2025 cuts to 4% and September/November holds, but not the December 2025 cut to 3.75%). Bank Rate is 3.75% today, the December cut was 5-4, and the OIS is trading around 4.11% at one year and 4.21% at two. That divergence is the substantive live point.

The HRA financing-cost ratio at 19.17% for 2025/26 (Table 1, p.5) is high in the library — HRA CFR is £304.7m servicing about £16m of financing cost against about £87m of net rents. Falling only to 16.31% by 2030/31, this is a long-term structural cost worth flagging alongside the mid-2025 HRA reform that opened the 40bp HRA discount on PWLB. And the strategy's stated flexibility on debt rescheduling (§7.1) implicitly assumes premiums on the book, when our indicative valuation at DMO notice 314/26 PM says 57 of 62 PWLB loans are at a discount, totalling £82.7m net or 21.3% of principal — driven by four sub-3% loans drawn 2020-2021 for 44-48 year maturities.

The loan-book reconciliation is not verifiable. The paper prints total external borrowing but no PWLB subtotal, no maturity profile, no weighted rate and no LOBO amount. Our file returns 62 PWLB loans totalling £388.4m at 3.51% at 31.03.26 — plausibly consistent with the £528.4m external total once c.£120m of visible market debt, c.£30m of LOBO and any short-term LA borrowing are added, but that's inference. Per PIPELINE.md, an unverifiable reconciliation is a failed reconciliation — the loan-book claim stays out of the email and the underlying figure stays in the note. The paper is nonetheless a full read on strategy and prudential indicators, and there is a strong hook without it. No officer addresses are published on any of the three appendix front sheets.

officer.body:
Hi [OFFICER NAME],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the 2026/27 treasury strategy that went to Cabinet on 26 January and Full Council on 12 February, currently in force, ahead of what looks likely to be the mid-year monitoring update your Treasury Management Practices set on a six-monthly cycle. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. The Appendix B(iii) balance sheet foots to the pound in every one of your six forecast years, and this is offered in that spirit rather than as a critique.

The reason we wrote is what your own arithmetic shows about the size of the bet in this strategy. Table 3 in Appendix B(iii) has external borrowing running down from £528.4m at 31 March 2026 to £431.4m at 31 March 2031 — a £97m reduction over five years, largely PWLB maturing naturally — while your CFR only drops from £692.7m to £646.7m over the same period. The gap is the growing under-borrowed position, and it moves from £23.6m at 31.03.26 to £127.6m at 31.03.31. Section 1.49 acknowledges the under-borrowed position; the plan quintuples it.

Section 5.1 is honest about the trade: rates are 'on a downwards trajectory' and the risk is if they rise instead. Section 5.2 sets internal borrowing as top priority and anticipates 'long-term borrowing rates to remain stagnant over the next few years.' Section 4.1 describes Bank Rate at 4% following the August 2025 cut and the September and November holds. Bank Rate is 3.75% today — the December cut was 5-4 with the minority favouring holding at 4.00% — and the market is trading the one-year SONIA around 4.11% and the two-year around 4.21%. Rates are lower than the strategy assumed at the short end, but the market is telling you they won't fall as far as central expectations. That divergence is the assumption the £127m under-borrowed position is priced against.

For the market you'd draw into, July's sector PWLB activity was around £368m across 33 loans from 19 borrowers at an average 5.02%. The month-by-month breakdown, split by HRA and General Fund and by council, is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity. What that page also shows is how much of the strain has moved to the inter-authority market when PWLB months go quiet — the LA-to-LA rate range this year has run from 4.15% (Gloucestershire) to 8.50% (Cornwall for four days), a distribution no single council sees from its own trades.

One on the HRA. Your Table 1 has the HRA financing-cost ratio at 19.17% for 2025/26, dropping only to 16.31% by 2030/31 — one of the higher HRA ratios we've read this year against Ealing, Camden and Somerset. Since June 2025 the PWLB has offered a 40bp discount on HRA borrowing at each fixing (the HRA rate), and City of London's paper is the one that most clearly frames its consequences for a stock-holding authority. It's not advice — every HRA business plan sits on top of decisions we don't see — just a rate we publish daily alongside the standard and certainty curves.

And on rescheduling. Section 7.1 refers to 'premiums incurred' as the constraint on switching long-term debt to short. Against the DMO's current premature repayment curve — notice 314/26 PM, our daily indicative — most PWLB books we price sit at a discount today, especially any low-coupon debt drawn in the 2020-2021 window. We publish a per-loan valuation of every council's PWLB book against the same curve at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis. Nothing follows from that: we don't sell treasury products, we model no MRP or accounting treatment, and only the DMO can quote a real settlement. The point is only that the sign on 'premiums' may have flipped for a lot of books, and that's worth watching alongside the £127m of borrowing your plan defers.

One caveat on our data — your paper doesn't publish a PWLB subtotal, a maturity profile or a weighted rate against Table 3's £528m external total, and our file for North Tyneside doesn't reconcile cleanly to a printed figure because there isn't one. So this note doesn't quote our loan-book totals back at you.

On training, four fit your strategy well. SONIA Forward Curve & OIS and Reading the PWLBpredict speak directly to the rate assumption in sections 4.1 and 5.2. The Capital Strategy is written for members and is the right frame for a plan that shifts £100m onto internal borrowing over five years. Intra-LA borrowing & lending markets fits your section 5.2 priority order where temporary LA borrowing sits at position two. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew

Sources: 2026/27 Treasury Management Strategy, Annual Investment Statement and Credit Criteria (Appendix C, doc 32978); Prudential Indicators 2026-2031 (Appendix B(iii), doc 32975); Treasury Management Practices 2026/27 (Appendix D, doc 32979) — all to Council, 12 February 2026.
